cited_evidence.text: Yield strength, σy, and fracture toughness, KJIc, are mutually exclusive properties in many structural materials,. The trade-off between these properties is particularly strong in the toughest materials, i.e., metals and their alloys. For example, CrCoNi-based medium/high-entropy alloys and cryogenic steels with face-centered cubic (fcc) crystal structures invariably are extremely ductile, i.e., they have a low resistance to plastic deformation. The fracture resistance of these alloys is driven by plasticity ahead of the crack tip, which requires a relatively low yield strength and extended strain hardening,. During plastic deformation, a crack acts as a source and sink of dislocations, which effectively blunts and shields the crack, which allows it to resist propagation, i.e., the intrinsic toughness of the material results in an excellent crack-initiation toughness (KJIc). AbstractCoCrNi medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) have attracted extensive attention and research because of their superior mechanical properties, such as higher ductility, strength, and toughness. This study uses molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to investigate the cutting behavior of a gradient nanograined (GNG) CoCrNi MEA. Moreover, it explores the influence of relative tool sharpness and rake angle on the cutting process. The results show that an increase in the average grain size of the GNG samples leads to a decrease in the average resultant cutting force, as predicted by the Hall–Petch relationship. The deformation behavior shows that grain boundaries are crucial in inhibiting the propagation of strain and stress. As the average grain size of the GNG sample increases, the range of shear strain distribution and average von Mises stress decreases. Moreover, the cutting chips become thinner and longer. The subsurface damage is limited to a shallow layer at the surface. Since thermal energy is generated in the high grain boundary density, the temperature of the contact zone between the substrate and the cutting tool increases as the GNG size decreases. decision.trend: Research on high-entropy alloys has been focused on understanding their mechanical properties, such as strength, toughness, and ductility. Earlier studies have explored the effects of composition, processing conditions, and microstructure on these properties. Recently, there has been a shift towards understanding the role of defects, such as grain boundaries and dislocations, in governing the mechanical behavior of these alloys. Additionally, researchers have started to investigate the potential of high-entropy alloys for specific applications, such as electromagnetic wave absorption and dielectric materials.
decision.unsolved: The mechanistic hypothesis governing the retention or loss of toughness in high-entropy alloys remains unknown. While earlier studies have identified various factors that influence toughness, such as grain size, composition, and processing conditions, a comprehensive understanding of the underlying mechanisms is still lacking. Furthermore, the development of high-entropy alloys with optimized toughness and other desirable properties, such as strength and ductility, remains a significant challenge.
decision.lever: investigating the effect of grain boundary engineering on toughness
decision.why: Given the current trend in research, the next logical step would be to investigate the effect of grain boundary engineering on toughness in high-entropy alloys. This could involve controlled experiments to manipulate grain boundary characteristics, such as grain size, distribution, and chemistry, and measuring the resulting changes in toughness. This approach would help to elucidate the role of grain boundaries in governing toughness and provide insights into the development of high-entropy alloys with optimized mechanical properties.
